pr_title: AtlasEngine: Fix bugs introduced in 66f4f9d and d74b66a
pr_body:
### Disappearing glyphs

We only process glyphs within the dirtyRect, but glyphs outside of the dirtyRect
are still in use and shouldn't be discarded. This is critical if someone uses
a tool like tmux to split the terminal horizontally. If they then print a lot
of Unicode text on just one side, we have to ensure that the (for example)
plain ASCII glyphs on the other half of the viewport are still retained.

### Black viewport after font changes

The cursor was drawn without a clip rect, causing the entire atlas
texture to be filled with black. This just so happened to work fine 
in Windows Terminal but relied on a race condition.

Closes #13490

## Validation Steps Performed
* Disappearing glyphs
  * Start `tmux` in `wsl`
  * Split horizontally with `Ctrl+B`, `"`
  * `cat` a huge Unicode text file on the bottom
  * Ensure ASCII glyphs in the top half don't disappear ✅
* Black viewport after font changes
  * Start `OpenConsole` with `AtlasEngine`
  * Open Properties dialog and click "Ok"
  * Viewport content doesn't disappear ✅

Coincidentally I noticed the same just yesterday. I find it easiest to reproduce by changing the font size in OpenConsole.

FYI you can run OpenConsole with AtlasEngine by setting `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Console\UseDx` to `2` (`DWORD`), setting `Host.EXE` as the startup project and launching it.

So this issue consists of two bugs:
* Rows outside of the `_api.dirtyRect` (i.e. rows that haven't changed) need to be pushed to the head of the LRU queue so that they don't get invalidated. For instance if you use `tmux` and only scroll the bottom half, the glyphs of the top half need to be retained in the texture atlas of course. I actually planned for that, but forgot to add it in my PR so this was easy to fix. I'm sure this is what causes most of the above issues.
* Hard problem: https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/commit/d74b66a0a7955de529f02fd394d6f6536a96e88c has a bug where just opening OpenConsole's Properties dialog and clicking Ok without changing anything causes the texture atlas to go all black. I checked it in QRenderDoc and the texture is absolutely blank (no alpha, no nothing).
  * Puzzling part 1: Reverting the changes to `AtlasEngine::_drawGlyph` doesn't work. No text is produced.
  * Puzzling part 2: The `ID2D1RenderTarget` must work in principle however, because it _does_ produce the cursor texture correctly. Only the text is gone. It can't be the `_r.brush` either because I'm recreating it whenever I recreate the `ID2D1RenderTarget`.
  * Puzzling part 3: It works when the size of the texture grows naturally (i.e. from 256x256 to 512x256). Hence, the bug must be related to or caused by `AtlasEngine::_recreateFontDependentResources()`.

These 3 `Buffer` changes should've been here all along. The 3 corresponding STL functions already do exactly the optimal thing: nothing for trivial types (i.e. leave the memory uninitialized) and properly construct/destruct the types if they're proper classes. And in case of `std::uninitialized_copy_n` in particular it already uses `memmove` for trivial types internally. Perfect!
This change allows us to construct a `Buffer<iterator>` which is an array of non-trivial types.

BTW/FYI: I didn't use `std::vector` and wrote `Buffer` instead, because I want to convey that these things explicitly _don't_ hold resizeable contents (in general). For instance I didn't want a `push_back` method on my viewport arrays - that wouldn't make sense so that always felt a bit wrong to me. It also doesn't initialize contents to zero, allowing rapid creation/destruction and you can specify a custom alignment (improves rendering perf by about 20% over `std::vector` IIRC).

We need to avoid measuring glyphs with DirectWrite as much as possible, due to its insufficient font fallback performance. While not tracking dirty rects improves performance for ASCII ¹, it would make eastern scripts very unpleasant to use.

Brahmi script as used in India for instance runs at approx. 100k-150k code points per second on my fairly powerful workstation, compared to approx. 9M code points per second for Latin scripts. While 100k code points per second _sounds_ much, that's only ~30 FPS at 120x30 with my CPU running at 5 GHz. This means we have to cache DirectWrite results as much as possible and thus requires this workaround.

¹ Approx. 1.5x with DirectWrite, approx. 2-3x with Uniscribe.
